Require Strong Passwords

Protect your business by requiring your team to use strong passwords and a password manager. 

Strong Passwords Mean More Secure Business Accounts 

Small to medium-sized businesses are frequent targets for cybercriminals, and weak or stolen passwords are one of the easiest ways they get into business accounts. In fact, many people still use weak passwords to protect important information. According to NCA’s annual Oh, Behave! survey, 35% of participants still use personal details, like pet names or family members, in their passwords, with Gen Z (52%) and Millennials (45%) leading the risky trend.  

Strong, unique passwords are the first line of defense against criminals, but for many businesses they are overlooked. Weak passwords can mean a weak link for criminals to hack into your business systems to try to disrupt critical infrastructure. 

The good news? You can significantly reduce risks by requiring employees to use strong passwords and a password manager.   

Set an example by using long, random, unique passwords on all your accounts and store them in a password manager. Work with your IT team or provider to require employees to take these actions to access business systems. Encourage your customers and vendors to strengthen their passwords too, especially when interacting with your systems.  

Encourage Strong Passwords in the Workplace 

Build a culture of cybersecurity by making strong passwords standard practice. To make accounts even more secure, always use phishing-resistant MFA along with strong passwords.   

Require strong, unique passwords. 

Protect your business by enforcing policies that require strong passwords. Strong passwords are: 

Long: At least 16 characters long (more is better) 

Random: A mix of upper/lowercase letters, numbers and symbols or a passphrase of 5–7 unrelated words 

Unique: Used for only one account

Many systems let you set password rules to enforce these standards. Speak with your IT department or security manager to set secure password requirements. Regularly follow trends to update employee/customer password policies where needed. 

For additional security, pair strong passwords with multifactor authentication (MFA), also known as two-factor authentication (2FA). MFA adds a critical layer of security even if a password is stolen. 

Provide a password manager.  

A company-wide password manager makes it easier for employees to follow best practices. It: 

Generates complex passwords 

Fills them in automatically 

Stores them securely

Employees only need to remember one strong master password for the password manager. This helps prevent password reuse, weak passwords and accidental breaches.  

As your business grows, consider moving to an identity and access manager (IAM) with single sign-on (SSO), which lets users securely access multiple systems with one set of credentials.  

Change default passwords. 

Many hardware and software products come “out of the box” with default usernames and passwords that are widely known and easily exploited. Default passwords may be printed on the device or listed online. Require staff to change default credentials before using systems.
